Uh this session as always is being recorded. This is the ITF Notewell. It's Thursday. You've all seen it. This covers uh the implications of you being here both in terms of what we expect from you in terms of conduct and legal and IP concerns. Read it if you haven't read it. By now, you all figured out how to use Meet Echo. But if you are here in the room, please scan the QR code on any of the mic stands or in the back of the room uh to register your your presence here at the meeting. If you have the full client on your laptop, make sure it is muted. If you are operating remotely and have any plans at all to speak at the mic, please use a headset if you can to avoid echo cancellation problems. Once again, it is possible to watch mock over mock. Uh here's the URL. Magnus is going to put it in the Zulip chat in just a moment. And um uh you will have to continue to use the MCO light client to do all the Q stuff etc. and participate in the chat but you can watch the actual video over mock which is pretty cool. Thanks to our friends at Medco who are mock enthusiasts uh for allowing this to happen. Of course if we can launch Mach over mock aren't we done? Can't we just ship it? [laughter] Allan says yes. >> [snorts] >> We're not done. [laughter] >> People can watch video over the internet now. So I guess we're done. Um this is the agenda for today. It is much shorter uh because we this is uh one of the focuses today is going to be to burn down some of the um everinccreasing mockt issue stack. Um, and we're also going to talk about some other uh I they're they're transport related. Um, they are currently sitting as extension drafts. Doesn't mean they'll forever be extension drafts, but they're certainly in the transport and so we want to talk about those issues. Would anyone like to bash this agenda or tomorrow's which is unchanged from Monday? Okay, that's the end of the presentation. So, uh, I think we'll hand it to Will. Thank you. Let me just get an audio check. Is everything can you hear me? >> Yes, we can hear you well. >> Okay, great. Thank you very much. Good afternoon everyone. I wish I was there but I am here as we said. Uh I'm going to present the section I'm will presenting the section on sendide track switching. Next slide please. >> You have slide control. Oh, I do. Nice. Uh, let me find it. Here I go. So, just a reminder for those who have been following along, uh, this is not new. We began it in February with a design team get together. We've had two implementations built, one by Cisco, one by Nokia. And at London, we we presented it and received a bunch of feedback. That feedback has been incorporated in the design. So I'm going to review what's been incorporated and uh present it for you today. You might wonder what happened to DTS. Well, we renamed it, right? So SSTS stands for sender side track switching. We felt this was a better name and descriptor of what the functionality is. It it can bring you serverside ABR if you want to give it a media vernacular, but we tried to keep it uh payload agnostic. So it's basically switching tracks on the sender or the publisher side. The largest change we've made is to accommodate different algorithms for switching. So as soon as we posted the one algorithm, everyone came up and said, you know what, if we involve uh client buffer levels or RT or some measure of the history or a new exponentially weighted average scheme that they have, we would get a better result. and and everyone's right about this. Uh and the point is there's many many features that you might want to add in the future and if we bake all of these permutations into an RFC, it's going to be huge and I believe brittle and it's not going to be very extensible because someone will invent a new way of doing it that's better. So we decided to separate the design into a base component which other algorithms can then extend. So we've taken our switching set assignment parameter which is how you add a subscription to a switching set. It now has only two required fields. The switching set ID which is the switching set you want to put it in and then an algorithm identifier. And this allows us to support multiple algorithms improved algorithms from the ones we have today or ones we can't even imagine today but want to implement in the future. And each of those algorithms can then define additional fields for the switching set assignment parameter. And to accommodate this field difference, we've added a new uh setup option called SSTS algorithms. So the server uh during setup can can list the SSTS algorithms that it supports and the client will then have knowledge of those algorithms and know that it can use it. And if the relay does not want to support SSTs, it can return an empty list that is perfectly valid. So you can turn it off if you want to. And we have an Ayana registry where you can register these new algorithms. And what we've done is define algorithm zero. So we make the the coreqt spec defines this baseline structure and then it also defines algorithm zero which is an an intentionally simple implementation and it doesn't mean that it doesn't work well. I we have two implementations that show it working. Uh but it can certainly be changed or improved under conditions in the future. But we're going to come out the door with a working implementation. Alan, are you in quue for clarification? >> It is a clarifying question. Are you intending that there can be multiple switching sets in the same session using different algorithms? >> Yes. >> Okay. Then >> I see no reason not to support that. We might have one that is biased for extreme low latency switching. We might have another that's biased for sixsecond switching and takes into account client buffers that don't really exist in a real-time environment. So >> in the same session like between between the same two endpoints you've got I've got one set of tracks I've got my audio tracks with algorithm one and my video tracks with algorithm too. >> Yes. >> Okay. Perfect. Okay. So as I mentioned we define a default algorithm zero. And this default algorithm immediately extends the switching set assignment parameter to add in the additional fields that we defined in the initial draft design and in the PR. So we've added throughput threshold uh set throughput fraction that has since been renamed weight. Uh this was a comment from Alan. So that change was made yesterday. Uh activate switching and set rank is actually no longer optional. It's a required because of the serialization of this uh parameter and these rules we presented in London they have not changed. So the the weights and the ranking you can set everything the same rank. You have a very simple scheme but this allows you for example to have three sets of three switching sets in in operation simultaneously. There might be video, audio and slides in a web conferencing scenario. And you can have under differing throughput availability, you can fail down. So you can always preserve this highest uh switching set here because it's got the the lowest rank. It's the most important. So it always gets allocated the bandwidth first and then the second one. And it can be that you run out of available bandwidth and you just don't deliver under certain scenarios one of your switching sets. This is again by design. Several comments were made about DDoS protection. And to try to head this off, we originally had two setup options which limited the concurrent throughput and the concurrent tracks that you could use with DTS. And I think Gwendel has written extensively on this and Gwendel is also right. This is a clear attack vector. However, setting up per session restrictions is trivial to bypass and this was this was commented a lot in uh London. If we set up a limit per session, you just open up more sessions and you bypass all our limits. So really we have to fall back on a relay it protecting itself. It has to look at its resources and it it has to irrespective of anything negotiated with the client uh protect itself from abusive behavior. So it is the consensus in London was to remove these two setup options. Um and it it it is an attack vector and relays amongst all the other things they have to do need to make sure that under a scenario where the client's giving very little traffic but is causing a lot of traffic to move in the network that uh they can recognize this and perhaps discontinue the session. Some other items we decided in London. So issue number one was do we need the ability to remove a subscription from a set without unsubscribing from that. In other words, I don't want to switch it automatically, but I just want to pull it out. No one could come up with an immediate use case for this. So for the simple algorithm number zero, you can't do that. But future algorithms can implement a more sophisticated removal mechanism if you like it. The second decision we made here was repeating the switch ID. This is this is repeated with each subscription that you make each time you pass that switching set assignment parameter. Was it a good design? And we decided yes because it avoids an extra RT and defining the set and then waiting getting a confirmation that the set's been defined and then being able to use it in a subscription. So we've kept this design and then there were also requests to add timeout and stability measures. Uh this came from the mocktail guys with their implementation experience and we're not going to add these to algorithm zero but again future algorithms can add more sophisticated algorithms and um you can quickly work yourself into corner cases with this. So I like the idea that we can have multiple algorithms and can experiment with different timeout and stability damping functions. So I believe uh this work is now represented as PR 1638. We've resolved the major issues and the comments with Shair including Allen's uh exuberant 24 comments that he wrote in an external Google doc. Those were all addressed yesterday and the day before. So that that is in there. We've implemented the decision and the changes in London and we have also resolved the merge conflicts. So I'm I'm here. I believe the PR is ready to be merged and I'm open up for comment in the remaining time that we have on SSTS. Let me just see if there's a comment from uh Alan for Q. Uh I have a question about I I don't remember [clears throat] any of the comments I left in the doc. So and but I thought you just said I thought on the previous slide you said you can't remove a track from a switching set in algorith. >> That's not true. You can by unsubscribing it. you unsubscribe the track and it gets >> but then I no but I thought that in the review maybe I left a comment about the fact that you I thought you said you can remove you okay maybe need to go back and reread the text so there should be no way to change the switching set ID of a subscription like you put it in and it's in you can't remove it you can unsubscribe from it that's it >> you can unsubscribe but you can't change the ID that it's subscribed to so >> I thought I saw a text in the PR that said you could about explained how to change the ID. So maybe maybe I'm misreading or maybe it's been updated. >> Yeah. >> Uh Ian, I think from a design perspective, this looks good. Um thank you for updating this. I have not reviewed the most recent PR, but I have reviewed prior ones. Um so I think I know we can go back and forth on that. Um, [clears throat] I actually was unclear about where we've landed on this about like whether we're supposed to be a PR or a draft. I I realize I don't want to go too far into process, but >> so editor I want to know >> we did do a consensus call that it was supposed to be a draft. That is the current state of what is supposed to happen. Like if you like this PR and you think it's ready and you guys have the four of you think it's great, then we could just do that. But or we could make him have it do it a draft. I don't we don't only have the discussion right now. I think we do it offline with Will. >> Okay. >> But yes, that is the correct state. >> I I don't like to be put in the subjective uh situation of rejecting or accepting things like this which like the working group might have strong opinions on. Like I'm happy to get it ready to merge into the draft and like of course we will do that. But like I would rather the call be made by the chairs, the working group, some larger group because I don't want to be on the hook for like saying either yes or no. Lastly, >> can I remind the room that we had this exact discussion in London and it was decided that because our charter requires us to implement some implementation of ABR on the server side that we could this was originally written as an external draft and then it was it was the request was rewrite it as a PR which was that what was done. So, if we look at the minutes for London, that was a decision taken in London. >> And I'm not arguing either way. I wrote the draft and then I wrote the PR. Um, if someone wants to take it out and make it a draft again, I'm okay with that. >> Okay. >> Yeah. I don't I don't want to wrap around the axle about this. Uh, it's entirely possible. I've forgotten something that happens all the time, unfortunately. If the editors would like us to do a consensus call to cover themselves on this and a person and they do feel it is ready, we are happy to do that. Um but we we could do that unless you don't do it here. Colin. Oh no, I'm sorry. Mike is next in the queue. >> Thank you. Um yeah, so I also had the draft question but we can discuss more offline. Um so uh the other thing that uh I was thinking as you were presenting these slides is on the DDOS uh topic it sounds like the intent is that we have recourse uh at the session level that we negotiate this in setup and if uh you don't like the limit then the the session dies. Is has there been any thought about uh something more granular than that? um to communicate limits, you know, once things are kind of in in flight, you've got maybe multiple switching sets or something going on. Um >> yeah, I'm I'm just trying to think about this more uh in terms of the implications for actual applications when you hit these limits. Um because I'm expecting that we will have limits in place that some applications may be running into. >> Okay, that that's a good question, Mike. So currently, yes, it's up the discretion of the relay implementation if it wants to kill the whole session or maybe just terminate the subscriptions that are involved in that switching set. >> So my my vote would be that it terminates the the offending subscriptions for a switching set that it feels has an asymmetric ratio. It's there's too much data coming in and not enough data going out. And that's the ratio I would monitor if I were building a relay. And we're not going to set that as a negotiated parameter because the client will just open up more and more sessions and and do you know accumulated damage on the relay. But uh I think the exist the the spec has existing mechanism for the publisher to terminate the subscription with with an appropriate message. So I I think that's what a relay could do in that situation. So how's Cisco? Uh thanks uh will for um updating the PR.
